title: When it flows (Berakhot 34b)
hookLine: Chanina ben Dosa prayed for the sick and knew when his prayer flowed freely
tomorrow: who stands where even the perfectly good can't?

cards: Some days a toast comes out of your mouth smooth, like it was waiting there. Other days every word catches. You notice the difference in your tongue before your head explains it.
So how could a sage tell his prayer for the sick got through? Chanina ben Dosa said he could feel it: by whether the words flowed in his mouth.

teach.b: Rabban Gamliel's son is burning with fever. He sends two scholars to Chanina ben Dosa to ask him to pray. Chanina goes up to his upper room, prays, comes down and says: go, the fever has left him.
They ask: are you a prophet? He says: I'm not a prophet, and not a prophet's son.
But I have this from my teachers: if my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know it's accepted. If not, I know it isn't. They write down the hour.
Back home, Rabban Gamliel tells them: at exactly that hour the fever broke, and he asked us for water. Then a second scene, all body.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's son falls ill, and he asks Chanina, his own student, to pray.
Chanina puts his head between his knees and prays, and the boy lives. Yochanan's wife asks: is Chanina greater than you? He says no.
He's like a servant who goes in and out before the king. I'm like a minister who comes in on business.
So here are two things the body does in this passage: words that run free in the mouth, a head bowed low to the knees. Notice what Chanina never claims. He says he's no prophet.
The flow was a sign he'd been taught to listen for, felt, not figured.

how: Jews pray for the sick by name, often in the Mi Shebeirach for healing said in synagogue, and many add personal words; Chanina ben Dosa's sign of a fluent prayer is taught in Mishnah Berakhot 5:5.

o: praying fast and smooth so that God can't miss the words
a prophet's vision that shows who will get well again
a prayer that runs free in the mouth, a sign Chanina was taught

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: the fever broke; he asked for water
I'm not a prophet, nor a prophet's son
a prayer fluent in the mouth
like a minister before the king

s: Chanina claimed to be a prophet who could see the future
asked straight out, he says he's not a prophet or a prophet's son.
for the second sick boy, Chanina prayed with his head between his knees
and the boy lived, the Talmud says.
Yochanan ben Zakkai says Chanina is greater than he is
he says Chanina is like a servant before the king, and he himself like a minister.

games.q: your friend is about to send a long apology she's rewritten five times. she reads it aloud to you and it sounds stiff. what would Chanina's sign suggest?
o: send it: what counts is that the words are correct, not how they feel.
rewrite it again until no one could find a flaw in it.
say it aloud until it runs free in her own mouth, then send that.
games.why: Chanina listened for whether the words flowed in his mouth, felt, not figured. it was his sign for prayer; the same attention to how words sit in the mouth carries over.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's sick. If your body allows, sit forward and let your head bow low toward your knees, the way Chanina prayed. Say their name softly, and notice how it feels in your mouth.

wordCard.voice: When it flows. Chanina's sign, taught to him by his teachers: a prayer that runs free in the mouth, from a man who said he was no prophet.

orig.note: Hebrew: fluent, running smoothly; 'if my prayer is fluent in my mouth' (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5).

carryVoice: Hold onto this: when it flows, it's felt before it's figured. Twenty-nine of fifty, done.

sources.ref: Mishnah Berakhot 5:5 (Chanina ben Dosa: if my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know it is accepted)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 34b (Rabban Gamliel's son; 'I am not a prophet nor a prophet's son'; the noted hour; Yochanan ben Zakkai's son, head between the knees; servant and minister)
